unit_label: CB Module D unit 2: constituents of the Indian financial system structure (courseware unit 12)

facts.statement: Genesis, structure and money market (courseware): the importance of developing an appropriate financial infrastructure in promoting economic growth; a well-functioning financial market enables efficient use of market-based instruments of monetary policy by improving interest rate signals; apart from enhancing the efficiency of monetary policy, deep and well-regulated financial markets promote mobilisation of domestic savings and improve the allocative efficiency of financial intermediation; strong domestic financial markets also act as a buffer against external disturbances and help in absorbing shocks to the domestic economy during times of crises. Genesis: the Chakravarty Committee (1985) was the first to make comprehensive recommendations for the development of the Indian money market; this was followed by the Vaghul Committee set up by the Reserve Bank to specifically examine various aspects for widening and deepening of the money market; following the recommendations of these two Committees, new initiatives were taken by RBI: Instruments such as the Certificates of Deposit (introduced in 1989), Commercial Paper (introduced in 1989), inter-bank participation certificates (IBPCs) with and without risk were introduced; the Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI) was set up in 1988 to impart liquidity to money market instruments and help the development of secondary markets in such instruments (the Reserve Bank disinvested its shareholding in DFHI in March 2003); in the case of call money the rates were freed in India before the deregulation of deposit and lending rates of banks; the financial market reforms followed a well calibrated approach, from the mid-1980s with initiation of several measures following the recommendations of the Committee to Review the Working of the Monetary System in India, 1985 (Chairman: Sukhamoy Chakravarty) and the Working Group on the Money Market 1987 (Chairman: N. Vaghul); in the aftermath of the balance of payments crisis of 1991, the Committee on Financial System (Chairman: M. Narasimham, 1992) started the point for gradual deregulation of the financial sector. Structure of financial markets: the financial system currently comprises financial institutions, financial markets, and financial instruments; the various segments of the financial market in India are the money market, the Government securities market, the foreign exchange market, the capital market, and the insurance market; while money, government securities and foreign exchange markets are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, the capital market falls within the purview of Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and the insurance market is regulated by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA); the development of the money and Government securities markets in India was triggered by three major developments: first, the replacement of automatic funding of the Government deficits through ad hoc Treasury Bills (which carried a fixed coupon rate of 4.6 per cent per annum from December 1974) by Ways and Means Advances (WMA) at interest rates linked to the Bank Rate in 1997 which led to greater market-fiscal deficit and fostered the development of the Government securities market; second, the introduction of an enabling institutional and legal framework and the development of an array of indirect instruments of monetary control such as the Bank Rate (re-activated in April 1997), the strategy of combining auctions, private placements, and open market operations in Government paper since 1998-99 and the adoption of the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) in June 2000; third, the setting up of an appropriate legal, institutional, technological, and regulatory framework. Money market: the money market is the most important segment of the financial system as it provides the fulcrum for equilibrating short-term demand for and supply of funds, thereby facilitating the conduct of monetary policy; it is a market for short-term funds with a maturity of up to one year and includes financial instruments that are close substitutes for money; the three broad functions: (i) to provide an equilibrating mechanism to even out gaps in the demand for and supply of short-term funds; (ii) to serve as a focal point for central bank intervention for influencing liquidity and general level of interest rates in the economy; and (iii) to provide reasonable access to providers and users of short-term funds to fulfil their borrowing and investment requirements at an efficient market clearing price. The Reserve Bank is the most important constituent of the money market; the money market falls under the direct purview of the regulatory framework of the Reserve Bank; the primary objective of the Reserve Bank operations in the money market has been to ensure that short-term interest rates and liquidity are maintained at levels which are consistent with the overall monetary policy objectives, viz., price stability, ensuring adequate flow of credit to the productive sectors and maintaining orderly conditions in the financial markets. During the 1990s, the participation in the call money market was widened to cover primary and satellite dealers (through primary dealers) besides other participants; while banks and primary dealers are permitted to lend and borrow in the market, other entities could participate only as lenders; following the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee (1998) and the Reserve Bank Internal Working Group to Examine the Development of Call Money Market (1997), steps were initiated to reform the call money market and make it a pure inter-bank market, in a phased manner starting from 1999; the smooth transition of the call money market into a pure inter-bank market (including primary dealers) was finally achieved by August 2005.

Treasury bills, repo, CP, CD and call money (courseware): in well-developed money markets, Treasury Bills are an integral part of money market operations; in the Indian context the role of Treasury Bill (an instrument of short-term borrowing by the Government) as a money market instrument was largely attenuated because of certain historical developments: first, the substantial creation of Treasury Bills which reflected the persistent deficits of Government had largely remained unfunded over the years; the Reserve Bank therefore held bulk of these Treasury Bills; second, the situation was accentuated by the fact that the discount rate on 91-day Treasury Bills had remained unchanged at 4.6 per cent since 1974 and remained totally out of alignment with other short-term rates; third, these Bills were freely rediscounted by the Reserve Bank; the banks used the Treasury Bill market essentially for parking funds for very short periods of one to two days and given the stipulation of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) as an average balance to be maintained, over a fortnight, there were very large and volatile fluctuations in investments of banks in Treasury Bills as also in the banks cash balances with the Reserve Bank; corrective measures were initiated (a) allowing the recycling of Treasury Bills and (b) the introduction of an additional two-tier rediscounting fee. The money market during the 1970s and 1980s was also characterised by poor liquidity, paucity of instruments and limited number of participants: the call/notice money market had a narrow base and limited number of participants (banks and two all India financial institutions); the interest rates in the market were also tightly regulated and controlled by a voluntary agreement between the participants through the intermediation of the Indian Banks Association (IBA); prior to December 1973 the call market rates were freely determined by the market as the rates touched a high of 25 to 30 per cent and remained at that level; the IBA intervened and brought some order in the market as it was felt that high interest rate over long periods would distort the entire banking system and militate against the basic objectives of planned credit allocation under an administered structure of lending rates; a ceiling of 15 per cent on call money rates was fixed by the IBA in December 1973; the ceiling was reduced in phases to 8.5 per cent by March 1978; the resurgence of inflationary pressures and the sharp upward movement in administered interest rates in 1979-80 necessitated an increase in the ceiling on call rates to 10 per cent in April 1980. Repo: the repurchase agreement (repo), a short-term money market instrument is used for smoothening volatility in money market rates by central banks through injection of short-term liquidity into the market as well as absorbing excess liquidity from the system; the Reserve Bank has been concerned with the use of repo as an instrument by banks or non-bank entities; in India, banks often entered buy back arrangements in respect of government and other approved securities and PSU bonds among themselves and with their large public sector and corporate clients until April 1987; the Reserve Bank issued certain guidelines, inter alia, prohibiting buy back arrangements in respect of corporate securities and bonds issued by public sector undertakings; from December 1987 the units of Unit Trust of India were not eligible as approved security for the purpose of entering into repo transactions; to ward off undesirable developments following the detection of large scale misuse of repos, banks were prohibited from entering Government and other approved securities with non-bank clients, while they could enter buy back arrangements with other banks (inter-bank) with effect from April 4, 1988. The money market in India witnessed significant progress particularly from the mid-1990s: introduction of new instruments and supplementary measures to add depth and liquidity to the market; the period mainly consisted of (i) Call/Notice Money, (ii) Term Money, (iii) Certificates of Deposit, (iv) Commercial Paper, (v) Treasury Bills, (vi) Repurchase Agreements (Repo), (vii) Interest Rate Swaps/Forward Rate Agreements, and (viii) Rediscounting of Commercial Bills; a significant development in the Indian money market has been the introduction of Rupee derivatives, i.e., Interest Rate Swaps (IRS)/Forward Rate Agreements (FRA) in 1999 to further deepen the money market and enable market participants to hedge their risks; in 2005 market participants were advised to use only domestic rupee benchmarks for interest rate derivatives; market participants were given a transition period of six months for using Mumbai Inter-bank Forward Offered Rate (MIFOR) as a benchmark, subject to review. Repo market reforms since 1999: widening of participants and instruments, institutional development and bringing uniformity in trading and accounting practices with the help of FIMMDA; the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd. (CCIL) was set up to make the repo operations efficient with adequate safeguards; the turnover in the repo market has shown an increasing trend on account of various factors such as introduction of Delivery versus Payment (DvP), permitting rollover of repos; the market repo rate ruled below the call rate during certain periods; effective February 23, 2003, based on the advice of the Technical Advisory Committee on Money and Government Securities Markets (TAC), repo eligibility was extended to select category of non-SGL account holders with adequate safeguards to ensure transparency in the delivery versus payment system; effective May 11, 2005, participation in market repo facility has been extended to non-scheduled urban co-operative banks and select entities. Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligations (CBLO) emerged as a promising instrument in the money market with a sharp increase in volumes; CBLO is unique to India; it was launched by CCIL in January 2003 for the benefit of non-bank participants who were either phased out of the inter-bank call money market or were given restricted access to the market or were unable to get fair quotes from larger market participants. Commercial Paper (CP): in India CP is issued by well rated corporate entities and financial institutions in accordance with the terms and conditions set out by the Reserve Bank; banks are the major investors in CP; the differential between CP rate and banks Prime Lending Rates (PLRs) has been the main drivers of CP market in India; banks have at times arbitraged between the call and the CP market by borrowing from the former market and lending in the latter as inter-bank call rates have generally tended to be lower than CP rates; corporates in India have preferred to resort to CP issuance as against borrowings from banks when money market rates were below the PLRs of banks; active secondary market for CP could not emerge in India due to the preference of investors to hold the instrument up to maturity owing to higher risk adjusted returns as against other instruments as well as the differences in stamp duty between different States. Important measures taken to activate the CP market were the delinking of CP from the cash credit limit in October 1997, further conversion of CP in October 2002 into a stand-alone product in demat form only and trading of CPs in dematerialised form only helped to lower transaction costs and reduction in stamp duty effective from March 1, 2004; large investment interest by mutual funds on account of Reserve Bank guidelines on non-SLR debt securities and policy induced phasing out of leasing and finance companies from accessing public deposits also spurred the CP market. Certificates of Deposit: since its introduction in 1989, several initiatives were undertaken by the Reserve Bank to provide flexibility and depth to the CD market; the secondary market for CDs has not developed in India due to the preference of investors to hold the instrument up to maturity due to the higher interest rates offered on CDs relative to retail deposits; the flexibility of CDs has improved over the years through measures reducing the minimum lock-in period and amount of issue; the facility to hold CDs in dematerialised form also gave thrust to the market. Recent: the recommendations of the Technical Group on Money Market (May 2005): the focus and policy thrust of the Reserve Bank in the money market has been towards encouraging the growth of collateralised borrowing and lending, developing the rupee yield curve, ensuring transparency and better price discovery, and improving risk management systems in money market operations; the FRBM is likely to reduce the supply of Government paper calling for broad basing the pool of securities to act as collateral for repo and CBLO markets; there are various issues relating to the OTC derivatives such as ambiguity over legality of such contracts, absence of netting laws, etc.; the amendment of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 to provide legal clarity on OTC derivatives assumes significance. Call money: the average call money rate ranged between 7 per cent (1993-94) and 17.7 per cent (1995-96) during the early 1990s fluctuated in a narrow range of 4.6 per cent to 9.2 per cent during 2000-01 to 2004-05 reflecting the comfortable liquidity; the Reserve Bank has attempted to ensure relative stability in call rates as reflecting the success of the liquidity adjustment policy through LAF; several factors like the overall liquidity, the size of the Government borrowing programme, growth in non-food credit, capital flows, tax outflows, seasonal factors and the Reserve Bank market operations influence the call money market; since integration of the various segments, call rates have been influenced by developments in forex, government securities and at times, in the capital market. The term money market (the market for short-term funds of over 14 days) has not yet developed notwithstanding several measures taken in the past. Even though banks were exempted from the maintenance of CRR and SLR on inter-bank liabilities from April 19, 1997, the average daily turnover in the term money market has not increased substantially.

Government securities market (courseware): the Government securities market in India forms an overwhelming part of the overall debt market; interest rates in this market provide benchmarks for other segments of the financial market. Historically the impetus for the development of the Government securities market in India has come from the large Government borrowing requirements while an additional reason during the 1990s was the increased capital flows and the need for sterilisation; the Reserve Bank used domestic eligible marketable bonds from its portfolio whenever it wanted, to sterilise the monetary expansion. The Reserve Bank actively operates in the gilt-edged market to create orderly conditions in the market by influencing the prices and yields of securities; under Section 17(8) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the Reserve Bank is authorised to purchase and sell securities of the Central Government, or a State Government of any maturity and the security of a local authority specified by the Central Government on the recommendations of the Central Board; however, at present the Reserve Bank deals only in the securities issued by the Central Government and not in those of State Governments and local authorities; the Reserve Bank derives its regulatory power over the Government securities market from Section 16 of the Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956, under which the Government has delegated the powers exercisable by it to the Reserve Bank. Previously, a deep and liquid Government securities market could not emerge (particularly from 1950s) due mainly to the heavy borrowing requirements of the Government and the artificially low coupon rates on Government securities; financing of the budget deficit of the Central Government by the Reserve Bank took place through an arrangement of automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills; to ensure absorption of the large supply of Government securities in the face of administered rates, the Reserve Bank mandated maintenance of a minimum statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) whereby the commercial banks had to set aside substantial portions of their liabilities in investments in Government securities at below market interest rates; the market was also characterised by a number of peculiarities such as voucher trading, switch quotas, cash purchase and separate purchase and sale lists. Historically, investors in the gilt-edged securities included individuals as well as financial institutions; over a period, the gilt-edged market had assumed the nature of captive market with the banks and financial institutions as the major subscribers; effective March 16, 1949, banks were required to maintain liquid assets in cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities amounting to not less than 20 per cent of their total demand and time liabilities (DTL) in India under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; the SLR was the outcome of the action taken to prevent banks from offsetting the impact of variable reserve requirements by liquidating their government securities holdings; the Act was subsequently amended in 1962 requiring all banks to maintain a minimum amount of liquid assets equal to not less than 25 per cent of their DTL in India effective from September 16, 1964; since 1970, the SLR has been gradually increased with the objective of restricting the expansionary trend in bank credit as also for augmenting banks investments in Government securities particularly in the context of financing of the Five-Year Plans; the Regional Rural Banks and cooperative banks were also required to maintain the SLR at the minimum of 25 per cent; subsequently the SLR has been frequently increased in the 1970s touching 34 per cent in December 1978, 35 per cent in October 1981, and further to 38.5 per cent in September 1990; over the years, efforts have been made to reduce the SLR in a bid to impart some degree of flexibility to the banking system; as on 08 October 2022, the SLR stood at 18 per cent of NDTL. The 1990s marked a watershed in the development of the Government securities market with wide ranging reforms in terms of instruments, institutions, and procedures: a major development in the market was the introduction of an auction system for dated securities in June 1992, which marked a move towards market related coupons on the Government securities; plain vanilla, fixed coupon bonds formed most of the Government bond issuances prior to the 1990s; an abiding objective of the Reserve Bank as the Government debt manager has been to evolve Government securities with new features to suit both the preferences of the Government as well as the market and in tune with evolving market conditions; the sale of Government securities in India has been done both through preannounced/tap issues; auctions were of the discriminatory/multiple price auction, sealed bid type; with a view to eliminating the problem of winner curse (i.e. French Auction) associated with the multiple price auction and broadening the market participation, the uniform price auction method was introduced in respect of 91-day Treasury Bill; Simultaneously, with a view to moderating the adverse impact of the large borrowing programme, the Reserve Bank began accepting private placement of Government securities and releasing them to the market as and when the interest rate expectations became favourable; as part of market development measures, a variety of Treasury Bills, viz., 14-day, 91-day, 182-day, 364-day maturities have been introduced; key instruments were also introduced at the longer end of the maturity spectrum during the 1990s; innovations were also introduced with respect to long-term bonds, such as zero-coupon bonds (January 1994), floating rate bonds (1995-96) and capital- indexed bonds (December 1997); bonds with call and put options were also introduced. Institutions: to develop the secondary market for Government securities, the Securities Trading Corporation of India (STCI) was set up by the Reserve Bank jointly with the public sector banks and all-India financial institutions in May 1994; as the market progressively reached higher stages of development, the Reserve Bank divested its holdings in the institution; the system of Primary Dealers (PDs) was also introduced in March 1996 to provide two-way quotes and develop the market; a delivery versus payment (DvP) system was introduced in transactions in the Government securities market from July 1995; to encourage the formation of mutual funds which are dedicated exclusively to investments in the Government securities, the Reserve Bank also introduced a liquidity support facility; to provide a safety net or exit route for PDs and to enhance their active market making role in Treasury Bills, effective February 2000, a conditional repurchase of Treasury Bills through OMO providing exclusive access to PDs; the Negotiated Dealing System (NDS) was operationalised since February 15, 2002, to provide, inter alia, an on-line electronic bidding platform for auctions in Central/State Government securities and OMO/LAF auctions; the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd. acted as the counterparty in all trades involving Government securities, repos, and foreign exchange; NDS-OM (an electronic order matching trading system) was incorporated into the NDS to facilitate anonymous secondary market trading in Government securities (from August 2005); the investor base: banks, cooperative banks, insurance companies, provident funds, financial institutions (including term-lending institutions), mutual funds, primary dealers, non-bank finance companies and corporate entities; banks have been the dominant investors in the Government securities primarily on account of SLR requirements; the share of commercial bank holdings of Government securities reached a peak of 72 per cent at end-March 1994 before declining to 58 per cent in end-March 2005; the commercial banks holding of Government securities as on March 31, 2017, stood at Rs.30,309 bn. and accounted for 40.46 per cent of total Government securities. Consolidation and other reforms: the Reserve Bank has been following a policy of passive consolidation of Government securities through the process of reissue of existing securities to improve market liquidity; of the 111 outstanding securities issued by the Central Government as on date, only 20 had a size of Rs 15,000 crore or more; re-issuance has achieved some degree of consolidation, but there are still many small sized securities; the Reserve Bank announced a Cash and Debt Management Group in May 1997; the Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy; the Reserve Bank has moved away from announcing the yield curve; FIMMDA announces yield curve data on a daily basis (from October 2000); measures included withdrawal of the 14-day and 182-day Treasury Bills coupled with a simultaneous increase in the notified amount of 91-day Treasury Bills (the 14-day bill was discontinued and 182-day bills were reintroduced in April 2005), a Negotiated Dealing System; a networked environment (INFINET); the Government Securities Act, 2006. Maturity profile: the average maturity of Government securities issued rose to 14.1 years in 2005 from 5.7 years in 1996; during 2021-22 about 58.2 per cent of market borrowings were raised through dated securities with a residual maturity of 10 years and above (the 30-year and 40-year securities were issued); the Reserve Bank assists State Governments in market borrowings; Ways and Means Advances (WMA) limits of the state governments were increased following the Advisory Committee on WMA. Recent developments: in April 2020 the G-sec yields hardened initially due to selling pressure from FPIs and expectation of increase in Government borrowing; special liquidity facility for mutual funds (SLF-MF); with effect from April 1, 2020, FPIs have three routes to invest in G-secs: the general route with investment limits set under the medium-term framework (MTF), the voluntary retention route (VRR) and the fully accessible route (FAR); FPIs also invested in G-secs during April 2020 to March 2021 through the VRR; the State Development Loans (SDLs) also witnessed FPI buying.

Foreign exchange market, benchmarks and the LIBOR transition (courseware): the foreign exchange market in India has witnessed a significant transformation from a highly controlled regime to a liberal regime; the forex market basically comprises of banks designated as Authorised Dealers (ADs), exporters and importers, individuals and the Reserve Bank; before 1990s, the market was highly regulated: banks, exporters and individuals had to surrender the foreign exchange earned/received by them to the Reserve Bank; following the reform process ushered in 1991 and with the transition to a market determined exchange rate system in March 1993, the forex market in India has acquired increasing depth and volume of operations. The mode of exchange rate determination: internationally the exchange rate regimes have witnessed significant changes; there is no single exchange rate regime which can be considered appropriate for all countries, at all times; the choice of an exchange rate regime is country-specific and contingent. The stance of policy before 1990s i.e., during the control regime was to manage the exchange rate mainly for facilitating India imports; the strict control on forex reserves under FERA had the dubious distinction of creating one of the largest and most significant parallel markets for foreign exchange in the world, i.e., the hawala (unofficial) market. For management of the foreign exchange reserves, the Reserve Bank has been empowered to buy and sell foreign exchange from and to scheduled banks, under Section 17(3)(a) of the RBI Act, 1934; the Government notifications under Section 40 prescribed the rates at which the Reserve Bank was bound to buy/sell Pound Sterling; the foreign currencies purchased by the Reserve Bank under this Section were Pound Sterling, US dollar (since October 1972), Deutsche Mark (since March 1974) and Japanese Yen (since end-May 1974); Pound Sterling was the only currency sold by the Reserve Bank up to February 1993 as it was the intervention currency; thereafter, the US dollar became the intervention currency; the agreement with the United Kingdom, which was initially for a period of three years, was renewed repeatedly until it was finally terminated on December 31, 1974; from October 4, 1975, the Reserve Bank has stopped announcing buying and selling rates for spot US dollars and stopped selling any foreign currency; in July 1978 the statutory provisions in the Reserve Bank Act were amended and enlarged to enable the Reserve Bank to utilise more effectively the foreign exchange reserves; the major banks started quoting two-way prices against the Rupee as well as in cross currencies (Eurocurrencies) in 1975 whereby the external value of rupee was determined by a weighted basket of the currencies of India major trading partners, de-linked from the Pound Sterling and under the managed floating arrangement; in 1981 the Guidelines for Internal Control over Foreign Exchange Business were framed for adoption by the banks. Reform period (1990s to 2010): the impetus for forex market reform was provided by recommendations of the Rangarajan Committee (1992), the Sodhani Committee (1995) and the Tarapore Committee (1997); the importance attached to the forex market is amply evident from the preamble to the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA, 1999); one of the main objectives of the FEMA is the orderly development of the foreign exchange market in India. In the early 1990s, the forex market was in the initial stages of development and suffered from several shortcomings: the spot as well as forward markets lacked depth and liquidity; the market was skewed with a handful of public sector banks accounting for bulk of the market business; from a managed floating system under which the exchange rate was officially determined, the regime had passed through several phases to reach a market-based system; radical changes in policy regarding the exchange rate of the Rupee were made in 1991: first, the rupee was adjusted downwards in two stages, on July 1 and July 3, 1991; on March 1, 1992, partial convertibility of the rupee was introduced in the form of a dual exchange rate system called the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS): all foreign exchange receipts on current account transactions (exports, remittances, etc.) were required to be surrendered to the ADs in full; the rate of exchange for conversion of 60 per cent of the proceeds of these transactions was to be at the market rate quoted by the ADs while the remaining 40 per cent were to be converted at the Reserve Bank official rate; the downward adjustment in the official exchange rate took place in early December 1992 and ultimate convergence of the dual rates was made effective from March 1, 1993; features of the modified LERMS: all foreign exchange receipts were converted at market determined rates of exchange from March 2, 1993; the unification of exchange rates marked an important step in the progress towards convertibility on the current account; the ADs were not required to surrender to the Reserve Bank any part of foreign exchange sold to them; from October 4, 1995, the Reserve Bank discontinued its buying and selling rate; at present, the Reserve Bank announces a Reference Rate based on the quotations of a few select banks in Mumbai at twelve noon every day; in order to ensure that the exchange rate of the rupee fully reflected the demand-supply situation, it was decided with effect from July 3, 1995, to reduce debt service payment (civil) of Government of India through the Reserve Bank. Current account transactions were freed of exchange control regulations; the Indian forex market has a floating rate with no fixed rate target; the Reserve Bank intervenes to prevent volatility and instability. Measures by the Reserve Bank: freedom to banks to fix overnight open position limits and gap limits, initiate trading positions in the overseas markets, determine the interest rates (subject to a ceiling) and maturity period of FCNR(B) deposits, use derivative products; ADs have been allowed to borrow abroad to relate their capital base as a prudential measure; corporates have been permitted to hedge anticipated exposures; various risk management strategies including freedom to cancel and rebook forward contracts, cost-reduction strategies like range forwards, and hedging of ECB exposures; Exchange Earners Foreign Currency (EEFC) account entitlement; CCIL commenced settlement of forex operations for inter-bank US Dollar/Indian Rupee spot and forward trades from November 2002 and inter-bank US Dollar/Indian Rupee tom trades from February 2004; the Technical Group on the Forex Market (2005) made various recommendations; the appropriateness standard for derivatives; derivatives accounting in India is still in the formative stage; CCIL settles all forex inter-bank cash, tom, spot and forward USD/INR transactions (from 1 December 2009 CCIL commenced settlement of forex forward trades with guarantee from the trade date). Capital account: capital account convertibility is virtually open in a de facto sense for individuals and non-financial firms; the Reserve Bank distinguishes between strategic controls on capital flows and tactical controls. Post reform period: the average daily forex turnover rose from approximately US$ 16 billion in 2005-06 to nearly US$ 55 billion in 2014-15; the depth of the market can also be gauged from the fact that the bid-offer spread in the USD-INR pair is quite narrow now; the forex market conditions have generally remained orderly with intermittent episodes of volatility; in August 2013 the rupee touched a historic low of 68.85 to a dollar (on August 28, 2013) after the possibility of early QE-tapering led to an exodus by FIIs; the measures taken by RBI and the Government (forex market intervention, monetary tightening through reduction in banks access to overnight LAF and increase in MSF rate, special concessional swap window for FCNR(B) deposits, increase in import restrictions on gold, tighter limits on overseas direct investment by Indian companies) stabilised the rupee; India reserves stood at around US$ 360 billion as at end-March 2016 and rose to US$ 576.9 billion as at end-March 2021; as at 07 October 2022 the reserves stood at US$532.838 billion. Financial benchmarks: financial benchmarks are indices, values or reference rates used for the purpose of pricing, settlement and valuation of financial contracts; the revelations regarding manipulation of LIBOR in June 2012 shocked the entire financial markets; the Reserve Bank of India set up a Committee on Financial Benchmarks in June 2013 (Chairman Shri Vijay Bhaskar) to review the existing systems around major financial benchmarks in India; based on the recommendations of the Committee, the RBI has designated FIMMDA and FEDAI as the benchmark administrators for the Indian rupee interest rates and Forex benchmarks respectively; the FIMMDA and FEDAI in association with IBA have formed a new entity called FBIL (Financial Benchmarks India Pvt. Ltd) in December 2014 as a private limited company under the Companies Act 2013; its aim is to develop and administer financial benchmarks relating to money market, government securities and foreign exchange in India; FBIL publishes benchmarks relating to overnight MIBOR, Term MIBOR, FC-Rupee Options Volatility Index, CD and T-Bill and Market Repo Overnight Rate; the February 2018 Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies proposed that (i) FBIL would assume the responsibility for standardising the valuation of Government securities (issued by both the Centre and States) currently being done by FIMMDA; and (ii) FBIL would assume the responsibility for computation and dissemination of the daily Reference Rate for Spot USD/INR and other major currencies against the Rupee. LIBOR transition: RBI has provided a Road Map for LIBOR Transition vide notification dated 8th July, 2021 requested to frame a Board-approved plan, outlining an assessment of exposures linked to the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) and the steps to be taken to address risks arising from the cessation of LIBOR, including preparation for the adoption of the Alternative Reference Rate (ARR); the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), UK has announced on March 05, 2021 that LIBOR will either cease to be provided by any administrator or no longer be a representative rate: (a) immediately after December 31, 2021, in the case of all Pound sterling, Euro, Swiss franc and Japanese yen settings, and the 1-week and 2-month US dollar settings; and (b) immediately after June 30, 2023, in the case of the remaining US dollar settings; banks/financial institutions are encouraged to cease, and also encourage their customers to cease, entering into new financial contracts that reference LIBOR as a benchmark and instead use any widely accepted ARR, as soon as practicable and in any case by December 31, 2021; banks/financial institutions are urged to incorporate robust fallback clauses in all financial contracts that reference LIBOR and the maturity of which is after the announced cessation date of the respective LIBOR settings; banks are also encouraged to cease using the Mumbai Interbank Forward Outright Rate (MIFOR), published by the Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd (FBIL), which is referenced to the LIBOR as soon as practicable and in any event by December 31, 2021; FBIL has started publishing daily adjusted MIFOR rates from June 15, 2021 and modified MIFOR rates from June 30, 2021 which can be used for legacy contracts and fresh contracts respectively.

payload.title: Why financial markets matter, genesis of the Indian money market and its structure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Importance:** a well-functioning market gives **efficient interest rate signals**, helps **market-based monetary policy instruments**, **mobilises savings**, improves **allocative efficiency**, and **cushions external shocks**.

**Genesis:** the **Chakravarty Committee (1985)** and the **Vaghul Working Group on the Money Market (1987)** led to the **Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper (1989)**, **inter-bank participation certificates** and the **Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI, 1988)**; the **Narasimham Committee (1992)** started gradual deregulation after the **1991 crisis**. **Call money rates** were freed **before** deposit and lending rates.

**Structure:** the **money market, Government securities market, foreign exchange market** are regulated by the **Reserve Bank**; the **capital market** by **SEBI**; the **insurance market** by **IRDA**.

**Three triggers for the money and G-sec markets:** (1) **ad hoc Treasury Bills (4.6 per cent coupon from December 1974)** replaced by **Ways and Means Advances (1997)**; (2) **indirect instruments** (**Bank Rate reactivated in April 1997**, auctions, private placements and OMOs from **1998-99**, **LAF in June 2000**); (3) a **legal, institutional, technological and regulatory framework**.

**Money market:** the **fulcrum for balancing short-term funds** (maturity up to **one year**), a **focal point for central bank intervention**, and a way for users to get **efficient prices**. The Reserve Bank is the **key constituent**. The call money market was made a **pure inter-bank market** (including **primary dealers**) in phases from **1999**, **completed by August 2005**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Indian money market grew from a narrow, administered market into a deeper market with several instruments.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two committees laid the groundwork for money market reform in the mid-1980s?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Chakravarty Committee (1985) and the Vaghul Working Group on the Money Market (1987).

payload.title: Instruments of the money market: Treasury Bills, repo, CBLO, CP, CD and call money
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Treasury Bills:** their role was **weakened** because bills created for **deficit financing** were **held by the Reserve Bank**, the **91-day discount rate stayed at 4.6 per cent from 1974**, and bills were **freely rediscounted**; banks used them for **one- or two-day parking**, causing **volatile balances**.

**Call money:** earlier a narrow market of **banks and two all-India institutions**; rates were controlled by the **Indian Banks' Association (IBA)** after rates hit **25 to 30 per cent**: a **15 per cent ceiling from December 1973**, cut to **8.5 per cent by March 1978**, raised to **10 per cent in April 1980**. Average rates ranged from **4.6 to 9.2 per cent in 2000-01 to 2004-05**. The **term money market (over 14 days)** stayed thin.

**Repo:** a **repurchase agreement**; misuse in the **1980s** (buy-back arrangements with non-banks) led to **rules from 1987-88** (no PSU bond buy-backs, **UTI units ineligible from December 1987**, banks barred from repos with non-bank clients from **April 1988**). **Reforms from 1999:** more participants, **delivery versus payment**, **rollover**, **CCIL** support, repo eligibility for select **non-SGL account holders (23 February 2003)** and **non-scheduled urban co-operative banks (11 May 2005)**.

**CBLO:** launched by **CCIL in January 2003** for **non-bank participants** shut out of call money; **unique to India**.

**Commercial paper (CP):** issued by **well-rated corporates and institutions** under RBI terms; **banks are the major investors**; driven by the gap between **CP rates and banks' PLRs**; **delinking from cash credit limits (October 1997)**, **demat-only (October 2002)** and **lower stamp duty (March 2004)** boosted it.

**Certificates of Deposit (CD):** introduced **1989**; **no strong secondary market** because investors **hold to maturity** for higher rates; **demat form** and **lower lock-in** helped.

**Derivatives:** **interest rate swaps and forward rate agreements (1999)**; from **2005** rupee benchmarks such as **MIFOR** only. **Technical Group on the Money Market (May 2005):** stress **collateralised lending**, **yield curve**, **transparency** and **OTC derivative legality**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The market deepened with new instruments, but secondary trading in CP and CD stayed thin.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation (CBLO).

payload.title: The Government securities market
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Role:** the G-sec market is the **overwhelming part of the debt market** and its rates are **benchmarks**. The Reserve Bank trades in **Central Government** securities under **Section 17(8) of the RBI Act**; its **regulatory power** over the market comes from **Section 16 of the Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956** (delegated by the Government).

**Pre-1990s:** a **captive market**: **administered low coupons**, **automatic monetisation** through ad hoc bills and a **statutory SLR** (**20 per cent from 16 March 1949 (Section 24, BR Act)**, **25 per cent from 1962/64**, then **34 per cent (Dec 1978)**, **35 per cent (Oct 1981)**, **38.5 per cent (Sept 1990)**; later lowered, **18 per cent of NDTL at 8 October 2022**).

**Reforms in the 1990s:** **auctions for dated securities (June 1992)** meaning **market related coupons**; **uniform price auction** for the **91-day T-bill**; **private placements** with the Reserve Bank for release when conditions were favourable; a range of T-bills (**14, 91, 182, 364 days**); new bonds: **zero-coupon (January 1994)**, **floating rate (1995-96)**, **capital-indexed (December 1997)**, bonds with **call and put options**.

**Institutions:** **STCI (May 1994)**; **Primary Dealers (March 1996)**; **delivery versus payment (July 1995)**; **liquidity support to gilt mutual funds**; **PD conditional repurchase of T-bills (February 2000)**; the **Negotiated Dealing System (NDS) from 15 February 2002** and **NDS-OM (August 2005)** for **anonymous order matching**; **CCIL** as **counterparty**; **FIMMDA** yield curve (**from October 2000**); the **Government Securities Act, 2006**.

**Investors:** banks (dominant because of **SLR**), co-operatives, insurers, provident funds, mutual funds, PDs, NBFCs. **Consolidation:** reissues to **build large securities** (only **20 of 111** securities were **Rs 15,000 crore or more**). **Maturity profile:** average maturity of issuance rose from **5.7 years (1996)** to **14.1 years (2005)**; **30-year and 40-year** securities followed.

**FPI access (from 1 April 2020):** the **general route**, the **voluntary retention route (VRR)** and the **fully accessible route (FAR)**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Auctions, primary dealers and electronic trading replaced administered pricing and a captive buyer base.

payload.title: The foreign exchange market, financial benchmarks and the LIBOR transition
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Before 1990:** a **controlled regime** with **surrender of foreign exchange** to the Reserve Bank; **FERA** policy created a big **hawala** market. The Reserve Bank bought **Pound Sterling, US dollar (October 1972), Deutsche Mark (1974), Yen (1974)** and sold only **sterling** (the **intervention currency**) until **February 1993**, when the **US dollar** became the intervention currency. From **October 1975** it stopped quoting spot dollar rates; the rupee was **de-linked from sterling** and tied to a **basket** under a **managed float**; banks began **two-way quotes (1975)**; the **1981 internal control guidelines** applied to forex business.

**Reform committees:** **Rangarajan (1992)**, **Sodhani (1995)**, **Tarapore (1997)**; **FEMA's** preamble stresses **orderly development of the forex market**.

**Exchange rate steps:** **July 1991** two-step **downward adjustment**; **1 March 1992 LERMS** (dual rate: **60 per cent at market rate** and **40 per cent at official rate**); **unification effective 1 March 1993**; from **October 1995** no Reserve Bank buying and selling rate, only a **daily Reference Rate** at **noon** from a few Mumbai banks; **July 1995** Government debt service payment made through the **market**.

**Liberalisation:** banks gained **freedom on position and gap limits**, **FCNR(B)** deposit terms, **derivatives**, **borrowing abroad within limits**; corporates may **hedge exposures**, **cancel and rebook forwards**, use **range forwards** and keep **EEFC** accounts. **CCIL** settles **USD/INR spot and forward trades (from November 2002)**, **tom trades (February 2004)** and **guarantees forward trades from the trade date (1 December 2009)**. The **appropriateness standard** guides **derivative sales**.

**Capital account:** **de facto open** for **individuals and non-financial firms**; the Reserve Bank separates **strategic** from **tactical** capital controls.

**Post reform:** daily turnover grew from about **US$ 16 billion (2005-06)** to **US$ 55 billion (2014-15)**; spreads are narrow; in **August 2013** the rupee fell to a low after **QE-tapering fears** and was stabilised by **forex intervention, tighter liquidity, a special FCNR(B) swap window and import restrictions on gold**.

**Benchmarks:** the **LIBOR manipulation scandal (June 2012)** led to the **Vijay Bhaskar Committee (June 2013)**; **FIMMDA** and **FEDAI** became administrators; **FBIL** was formed in **December 2014** (a **private limited company** with **FIMMDA, FEDAI and IBA**) to **develop and administer benchmarks** (**overnight and term MIBOR, CD and T-bill rates, market repo overnight rate, FC-rupee options volatility index**, and later **G-sec valuation** and the **daily USD/INR reference rate**).

**LIBOR transition:** the Reserve Bank asked firms to prepare **Board-approved plans**, stop **new LIBOR contracts**, add **fallback clauses** and prefer **alternative reference rates**; **LIBOR settings ceased or lost representativeness after 31 December 2021 (non-dollar and some dollar settings)** and **after 30 June 2023 (the remaining dollar settings)**; **MIFOR**, which references LIBOR, was to be replaced by **adjusted and modified MIFOR** from **June 2021**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: India shifted from a controlled exchange rate to a market-determined rate with deep spot and forward markets.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd; it develops and administers financial benchmarks for money, government securities and foreign exchange markets.
